title: India's Women's Cricket Revolution: How the Game Has Been Transformed
summary: Women's cricket in India has undergone a transformation in the past decade. With growing crowds, rising stars, and a World Cup final to their name, the Indian women's team is now one of the most exciting in world cricket.
content:
Cricket in India has always been a religion. The men's team is followed with an intensity that few sports rivalries anywhere in the world can match. But for most of cricket's history in the country, that devotion extended only so far — the women's game was an afterthought, underfunded, under-watched, and undervalued.

The past decade has changed that. Gradually at first, then rapidly, women's cricket in India has undergone a transformation that few would have predicted and that has permanently altered the landscape of the global game.

The 2017 Moment

The turning point was the 2017 Women's World Cup final at Lord's. India, rank outsiders, reached the final of the tournament played in England and faced the hosts at the home of cricket. They lost, in heartbreaking circumstances, by nine runs. But the team that walked off the field at Lord's had done something more significant than win a trophy: they had captured the imagination of an entire nation.

Mithali Raj, the captain, and Jhulan Goswami, the fast bowler who had carried Indian women's cricket for a decade, became household names overnight. The final was watched by hundreds of millions of people across India. And the BCCI — the most powerful cricket board in the world — took notice.

The Investment That Followed

What followed was unprecedented investment in the women's game. Central contracts, introduced in 2018, gave the top players financial security for the first time. Training facilities improved. The tour schedule expanded. And crucially, the Women's IPL — launched in 2023 with five franchises and broadcast on the same platforms as the men's game — created a commercial structure that could sustain the sport long-term.

The Women's IPL was not simply a good idea. It was a transformative one. With the resources of India's richest sports franchises behind it, the tournament attracted international stars, created rivalries that fans could follow across a full season, and gave young Indian players exposure to world-class cricketers at an age when it could genuinely accelerate their development.

When I started playing cricket, nobody cared. The ground was empty, there was no coverage, there was no money. What these young players have now — the crowds, the TV deals, the IPL — it is extraordinary. The game has been transformed in a way that I never imagined possible. — Jhulan Goswami

The New Generation

The generation that has emerged in the wake of that 2017 final is extraordinary. Smriti Mandhana — left-handed, elegant, capable of dismantling any bowling attack — is one of the most watchable batters in world cricket. Shafali Verma brings a fearlessness at the top of the order that has drawn comparisons to the great attacking openers of the men's game. Deepti Sharma is a world-class allrounder, capable of winning matches with both bat and ball.

These players have grown up in a different cricket culture than their predecessors — one where their sport is valued, where their achievements are celebrated, and where the financial rewards reflect their status as elite athletes.

What Still Needs to Change

Progress has been extraordinary, but the work is not done. Pay parity with the men's game remains a distant prospect. The number of matches the women's team plays annually still lags behind the men's. And at the grassroots level — in the villages and small towns where cricket is first learned — the infrastructure for girls who want to play the game still lags behind what their brothers and fathers enjoy.

But the direction of travel is unmistakable. Indian women's cricket is no longer an afterthought. It is a story — and one that is nowhere near finished.
